Pudding is a soft, cooked food. Whatever form it takes, it is always soft in texture — never crunchy, never dry. But beyond that single shared quality, the word means very different things depending on where you are in the world.

British English uses "pudding" in two ways.

1. Any dessert, informally

British people very commonly use "pudding" as a casual word for dessert — whatever sweet thing you eat at the end of a meal. If someone in Britain says, "What's for pudding tonight?", they simply mean, "What's for dessert?" It doesn't matter whether the dessert is a cake, a tart, ice cream, or a bowl of fruit — any of these can be called "pudding" in this informal sense.

2. A specific class of cooked dish

More precisely, a pudding in British cooking is a dish prepared by steaming or boiling a batter or dough, usually inside a bowl or cloth. This method produces a soft, dense, moist texture that is different from a baked cake.

The most important thing to understand here is that British puddings can be sweet OR savory. This surprises many learners.

Sweet British puddings:

  • Christmas pudding — a very dark, dense pudding packed with dried fruit (raisins, currants, etc.) and steamed for many hours. It is the traditional dessert on Christmas Day in Britain. It is rich, heavy, and often served with cream or brandy butter.
  • Sticky toffee pudding — a soft, warm sponge pudding covered in a thick toffee sauce. One of the most popular puddings in British restaurants.
  • Treacle pudding — a steamed sponge pudding poured with treacle (a thick, dark British syrup similar to molasses).
  • Bread and butter pudding — slices of buttered bread layered in a dish, then baked in a mixture of eggs and milk until set. It is soft, slightly custardy inside, with a golden top.
  • Rice pudding — rice cooked very slowly in milk and sugar until the whole mixture becomes thick and creamy. It is eaten warm or cold.

Savory British puddings:

  • Yorkshire pudding — this is the one that surprises people the most. It is a light, hollow, baked pastry shell made from a thin batter of eggs, flour, and milk. It is not sweet at all, and it is traditionally eaten alongside roast beef and gravy on a Sunday. It puffs up dramatically in the oven and becomes crispy on the outside, soft inside.
  • Black pudding — a type of thick sausage made from pig's blood, pork fat, and grain (usually oatmeal or barley). It is dark in color because of the blood, which is where it gets its name. It is a common part of a traditional British cooked breakfast.
  • White pudding — very similar to black pudding but made without blood, so it is paler in color. The flavor is milder.
  • Steak and kidney pudding — a savory filling of beef and kidneys cooked inside a casing of suet pastry (pastry made with animal fat), all steamed together. It is a hearty, old-fashioned British comfort food.

Why do savory foods carry the name "pudding"? Historically in Britain, the word described the cooking method — specifically, cooking food inside a bag, casing, or bowl by boiling or steaming. The flavor (sweet or savory) was not part of the definition. Over time, the word stuck to both sweet and savory dishes that were prepared this way.

In the United States, "pudding" has a much narrower and more specific meaning. It refers to a smooth, creamy, thick, sweet dessert made by gently cooking milk (or cream) together with sugar and a thickening agent — usually cornstarch — until the mixture thickens and sets into a soft, spoonable consistency.

American pudding is:

  • Always sweet
  • Always smooth and creamy (not chunky, not bready)
  • Usually eaten cold, served in a cup or bowl
  • Made in flavors like chocolate, vanilla, butterscotch, and banana

This is the type of pudding that comes in small cups in American grocery stores, or in powder form (called instant pudding) that you mix with cold milk and it thickens on its own without cooking.

American pudding is close in nature to what the British call custard — though they are not quite the same. Custard is usually made with egg yolks, which gives it a richer, silkier quality. American pudding is more often thickened with cornstarch, which gives it a slightly different, smoother consistency.

Tapioca pudding is eaten in both Britain and America, and it deserves a separate mention because it is unlike other puddings in texture. It is a sweet, creamy dessert made with tapioca pearls — small, round, chewy balls made from the starch of the cassava root. The pearls do not dissolve when cooked; they remain as soft, slightly bouncy little spheres suspended in a creamy sauce. The texture is unusual compared to smooth puddings like chocolate or vanilla — it has a characteristic "bubble-like" feel that people either love or find odd.
The one thing all puddings share

Across all these different uses — British, American, sweet, savory — every pudding is:

  1. Cooked (never raw)
  2. Soft (never hard or crunchy)
  3. Moist (never dry)

Whether it is a silky chocolate dessert in an American refrigerator, a dense steamed Christmas pudding in a British kitchen, or a crispy-outside, soft-inside Yorkshire pudding next to a roast, the softness and the fact of being cooked connect them all under this one word.

British "pudding" means:

  • (Informal) any dessert at the end of a meal
  • (Specific) a steamed, boiled, or baked dish — which can be sweet or savory

American "pudding" means:

  • A smooth, creamy, sweet dessert made with milk, sugar, and a thickener

If you are reading British literature, watching a British TV show, or speaking with a British person, remember that when they say "pudding," they might mean anything from a blood sausage to a Christmas dessert to simply whatever sweet thing is being served that evening. If you are in an American context, "pudding" almost certainly means the smooth, creamy, sweet stuff eaten cold from a spoon.
